column1: Family and community|Which classroom activity respects different family structures?|Invite children to describe the people who care for them without requiring one family pattern|Insist every child has identical relatives|Rank families by income|Require children to disclose private conflicts|Families and caregiving arrangements vary. Inclusive activities avoid defining one structure as the only valid one.

Family and community|Why should an EVS teacher avoid assigning occupations solely by gender?|Occupations are not determined by gender|Only men can be nurses|Only women can drive buses|Every occupation requires identical training|Examples should represent varied roles and challenge stereotypes rather than reinforce them.

Family and community|What is the best purpose of interviewing a local craftsperson in EVS?|Understand work, materials and community knowledge|Collect private financial records|Prove textbooks are always wrong|Replace all classroom learning|Community interviews connect school learning with lived experience; plan respectful questions and consent.

Family and community|A child cannot bring a family photograph. Which response is inclusive?|Allow a drawing or another chosen representation|Exclude the child from the activity|Lower the child's mark automatically|Demand an explanation in front of the class|Flexible alternatives maintain the learning goal without requiring disclosure or a particular resource.

Family and community|How should an EVS activity discuss disability?|Focus on accessibility, participation and respect|Define a person only by a disability|Use disability as an insult|Assume everyone requires the same adjustment|Accessibility and dignity should guide examples; support needs vary across individuals and contexts.

Plants|What do roots mainly help a plant obtain from soil?|Water and mineral ions|Only sunlight|Only oxygen for every plant process|Ready-made flowers|Roots anchor plants and take up water and mineral ions; leaves perform much photosynthesis.

Plants|Which part of many green plants is a major site of photosynthesis?|Leaves|Only seeds|Only flower petals|Only dry bark|Green leaves contain chlorophyll and receive light; some other green plant parts can also photosynthesize.

Plants|Why are seeds dispersed away from a parent plant?|It can reduce competition and help plants reach new places|It always prevents germination|It stops plants needing water|It makes every seed identical|Dispersal can spread offspring across suitable locations and reduce local competition.

Plants|Which condition is ordinarily needed for germination of a viable seed?|Suitable water, oxygen and temperature|Continuous fertilizer without water|Complete absence of oxygen for all seeds|Only a painted pot|Germination depends on suitable conditions. Light requirements differ among seeds, so avoid universal claims about light.

Plants|Which activity best helps children study leaf diversity?|Compare collected fallen leaves using shape, texture and veins|Memorize one leaf drawing as every species|Remove all leaves from living trees|Assume every leaf has the same shape|Observation and comparison help learners describe variation; collect safely and avoid damaging plants.

Animals|Which adaptation helps a camel move over loose desert sand?|Broad padded feet|Fish gills|Feathered wings|A flat swimming tail|Broad padded feet distribute weight on sand. Adaptations should be related to function and habitat.

Animals|How do gills help most fish?|Extract dissolved oxygen from water|Create freshwater from seawater in every fish|Replace every digestive organ|Allow photosynthesis|Gills exchange gases with water; breathing and feeding are different functions.
Animals|Which animal is a herbivore?|Deer|Tiger|Eagle|Crocodile|A herbivore feeds mainly on plant material; ecological diets can still vary by species and context.

Animals|What is a food chain useful for showing?|A sequence of feeding relationships|A complete description of every ecosystem interaction|Only the age of animals|Only rainfall changes|A food chain represents one feeding pathway. Food webs describe interconnected pathways more fully.

Animals|Which action is most appropriate during a school nature walk?|Observe animals without disturbing nests or feeding wildlife|Handle every unknown animal|Remove nests for display|Chase animals to record faster movement|Responsible observation protects learners and habitats while supporting inquiry.

Food|Which food is commonly a source of dietary carbohydrate?|Rice|Pure salt|Drinking water|Cooking oil only|Rice contains starch, a carbohydrate. Foods can contain several nutrients rather than exactly one.

Food|Which food group commonly supplies protein?|Pulses|Refined sugar only|Pure salt|Water only|Pulses contain protein along with other nutrients. Discuss diverse affordable sources without ranking families.

Food|Why is a balanced diet discussed in EVS?|Different nutrient groups contribute to bodily needs|One food always supplies every nutrient in ideal amounts|Only expensive foods are useful|Water has no role in the body|A balanced diet includes suitable variety; examples should respect local foods and avoid personal medical prescriptions.

Food|What is the main purpose of drying food for preservation?|Reduce moisture available for spoilage processes|Add unlimited protein|Change every food into a mineral|Make food immune to all contamination|Drying reduces water availability, but storage hygiene and conditions still matter.

Food|Why does refrigeration slow spoilage of many foods?|Lower temperature slows many microbial and chemical processes|It permanently sterilizes every food|It adds oxygen to all food|It guarantees safe storage indefinitely|Refrigeration slows processes rather than making food indefinitely safe. Follow suitable handling and storage guidance.

Food|Which lesson approach best connects food with community diversity?|Compare local food habits respectfully and discuss available ingredients|Declare one community's food inferior|Require everyone to eat the same food|Rank children by lunch cost|Food choices reflect environment, culture, availability and preferences; comparison should avoid stigma.
Water|Which process turns liquid water into water vapour?|Evaporation|Condensation|Freezing|Sedimentation|Evaporation is liquid-to-vapour change; condensation is the reverse transition.
Water|Which process forms liquid droplets from water vapour?|Condensation|Evaporation|Melting|Filtration|Cooling water vapour can produce liquid droplets through condensation.

Water|Which method removes suspended insoluble particles from water?|Filtration|Adding paint|Stirring indefinitely|Calling every clear liquid pure|Filtration can remove suspended particles; it does not by itself remove every dissolved contaminant or microorganism.

Water|Why is clear-looking water not necessarily safe to drink?|Some contaminants are not visible|Every contaminant is brightly coloured|Clear water cannot contain microorganisms|Only cloudy water can be unsafe|Appearance alone cannot establish safety. Use appropriate water-quality and treatment guidance.

Water|What does rainwater harvesting aim to do?|Collect and manage rainwater for use or recharge|Create rain on demand|Remove all natural drainage|Replace every water source permanently|Harvesting captures rainfall and can support storage or groundwater recharge when correctly designed.

Water|Which classroom investigation best compares water use?|Record measurable use for selected activities and discuss ways to reduce waste|Guess a household's income|Assume all homes have the same supply|Publish children's private addresses|Measurement and discussion support inquiry without requiring private household details.

Shelter|Why do houses differ between regions?|Climate, materials, terrain and social conditions vary|One house design is suitable everywhere|All regions have identical rainfall|Only paint colour matters|Shelter reflects environmental and human factors; avoid ranking communities by house appearance.

Shelter|Why can sloping roofs be useful in areas with heavy rain?|They help water drain away|They prevent all earthquakes|They generate drinking water automatically|They eliminate the need for walls|A sloping roof assists drainage; many other design factors affect safety and suitability.

Shelter|What is ventilation in a building?|Exchange of indoor and outdoor air|Only adding more furniture|Only painting walls|Blocking every opening|Ventilation supports air exchange; appropriate designs depend on climate, safety and occupancy.

Shelter|Which approach is suitable when discussing homelessness in EVS?|Use respectful language and discuss needs and support|Blame every individual|Ask children to mock affected people|Treat housing as unrelated to human needs|Housing is connected with social conditions and dignity. Classroom discussion should avoid stigma or forced disclosure.

Travel|What is the purpose of a map legend?|Explain symbols used on the map|Set every place's population|Prove the map is always current|Show only the mapmaker's signature|A legend connects symbols with meaning; read it together with orientation and scale.
Travel|On a north-up map, which direction is opposite east?|West|North|South|Northeast|East and west are opposite directions; north and south form the other principal pair.

Travel|What does map scale relate?|Distance on a map to distance on the ground|Height to temperature|Rainfall to food prices|Population to colour automatically|Scale is a ratio between represented and real distance; units must be consistent.
Travel|Which transport mode normally runs on fixed railway tracks?|Train|Bicycle|Boat|Aeroplane|A train runs on tracks; compare modes by route, capacity and suitability rather than only speed.

Travel|Why should a local-area walk have a clear safety plan?|Learners need supervision, accessible routes and agreed boundaries|Safety prevents all learning|Only the fastest walkers matter|Unknown hazards make activities better|Field learning requires appropriate planning, permissions and supervision so participation is safe and accessible.

Making things|Which activity best explores how materials affect an object's use?|Compare absorbency or strength using simple safe tests|Memorize brand names only|Assume every material has identical properties|Handle hazardous chemicals without guidance|Comparing properties connects material choice with purpose; use safe age-appropriate tests.

Making things|Why can reusing a container reduce waste?|It extends the container's useful life before disposal|It makes all waste disappear|It guarantees no cleaning is needed|It always uses more material than a new container|Reuse can reduce demand for new items; suitability, hygiene and safety must be considered.

Making things|What distinguishes recycling from reuse?|Recycling processes material into a new product|Recycling means using an item unchanged|Reuse always melts the material|Both always involve the same industrial process|Reuse uses an item again; recycling reprocesses material, often involving collection and sorting.

Making things|Which question promotes inquiry about a handmade basket?|How do the material and weaving pattern affect its strength?|What is the maker's private bank balance?|Which child owns the most expensive basket?|Can we memorize the price without examining it?|Questions linking structure, material and function support investigation and respect craft knowledge.

Teaching|What is the strongest reason for integrating EVS topics?|Real-life experiences connect natural and social aspects|It removes every need for subject knowledge|It guarantees every child has the same experience|It means no learning goals are needed|Integrated EVS connects living things, environment, community and human activity through meaningful contexts.

Teaching|Which starting point is often useful for primary EVS?|Children's local experiences and questions|Only distant technical terminology|Only definitions copied silently|Only adult assumptions about children's lives|Familiar experiences support observation and questioning while teaching broadens understanding beyond the local context.

Teaching|What should a teacher do when children's observations conflict?|Help them compare methods, evidence and conditions|Declare the first answer always correct|Punish both groups|Ignore evidence|Differences can arise from conditions or observation methods. Comparison develops inquiry and reasoning.

Teaching|Which assessment best captures observation skills?|Observe a learner describe and compare actual specimens|Use only a handwriting speed test|Use only attendance|Use only copying of a printed definition|Assessment should align with the intended skill and include evidence of the learner's process.

Teaching|How can a concept map help EVS learning?|Show relationships among ideas|Replace all observations permanently|Measure only spelling speed|Guarantee every link is scientifically correct|Concept maps make relationships visible; teachers and learners should discuss and revise unsupported links.

Teaching|Which field-trip follow-up best supports learning?|Organize observations, discuss evidence and reflect on questions|Discard all notes|Test only the bus registration number|Avoid connecting the visit with class topics|Reflection connects field experience to concepts and makes unanswered questions explicit.

Teaching|Why should EVS worksheets include varied representations?|Learners can demonstrate understanding through words, drawings, sorting or explanations|Every child must use the identical format|Pictures always replace all reasoning|Only fluent writers can understand EVS|Varied representations reduce irrelevant barriers and provide different evidence of understanding.

Teaching|What is an appropriate use of a local resource person?|Plan relevant questions and acknowledge expertise respectfully|Treat the person as a source of private information|Assume community knowledge never has limitations|Cancel all other sources|Resource people connect classroom learning with experience; compare claims with evidence where appropriate.

Teaching|What should a teacher do with a child's incorrect explanation of floating?|Use safe comparisons to investigate the child's rule|Simply label the child unintelligent|Avoid all experiments|Tell the child never to explain ideas|Testing varied objects can help learners revise simple rules; mass alone does not determine floating.

Teaching|Which statement best describes a good EVS question?|It can encourage observation, comparison and evidence-based explanation|It must always have the longest wording|It should always require a costly resource|It should discourage any follow-up question|Good inquiry questions connect evidence with reasoning and can open productive further investigation.
